facts: A package declares a dependency when it needs another package on disk at runtime, such as a runtime or toolchain. [L6]
OCX resolves the graph at install, hardlinks dependency content into the consumer, and composes env per the chosen visibility. [L6]
Bundling ships a dependency's bytes inside your archive, while depending points at another package by digest and shares one install. [L10]
Declare a dependency when it is large or common, when you need a specific upstream version, or when your package runs it. [L12]
Bundling Node.js into every npm wrapper would re-ship about 30 MB per package, while a declared dependency is installed once and shared. [L14]
A wrapper that shells out to cmake reaches it through the installPath placeholder, which gives its location on disk. [L16]
Bundling stays right for tiny, single-use, or version-coupled dependencies such as a patched vendored library. [L18]
Every published dependency is pinned by OCI digest, never by version range or floating tag. [L22]
The digest must reference a platform manifest, never an OCI Image Index, which 404s once the publisher pushes again. [L22]
While authoring, a dependency identifier needs only an explicit registry, and the digest is optional. [L24]
The first JSON example shows a tag-only dependency with an explicit registry and public visibility, the form written before create. [L26]
The create command with a platform flag resolves each tag-only dependency against the selected index and rewrites the sidecar with the pin. [L34]
The second JSON example shows the same dependency after create, now carrying a sha256 digest. [L36]
Commit the sidecar that create rewrote and push it with the archive, since push makes no resolution decisions. [L44]
Push refuses with exit 65 any dependency that is tag-only, index-pinned, or missing a pin for its platform. [L44]
Create with remote goes straight to the registry, while offline or frozen refuse an uncached tag with exit 81. [L46]
The default resolves locally first and falls back to a fetch, and a tag missing from the index fails with exit 79. [L46]
Every dependency identifier carries an explicit registry, and the digest becomes mandatory once the package is published. [L48]
An any-platform package can depend only on a dependency that also offers an any manifest. [L52]
A dependency with only platform-specific manifests fails create with exit 65, and the error names the dependency. [L52]
By default the placeholder name is the last path segment of the repository, which collides when two dependencies share it. [L56]
The name override example gives two cmake dependencies distinct keys, myorg_cmake and cmake, used by separate env entries. [L58]
A name override must match lowercase letters, digits, underscore or hyphen and stay at most 64 characters. [L71]
Identifiers always carry an explicit registry, and a digest without a registry is rejected. [L71]
Edge visibility on a dependency entry is separate from entry visibility on env entries. [L75]
Sealed is the default and exposes the dependency env on neither surface; the content is reached only by installPath. [L78]
Private exposes the dependency env to the package's own runtime but not to consumers. [L79]
Public exposes the dependency env to both the package and its consumers. [L80]
Interface forwards the dependency env to consumers only, for meta-packages that do not use it themselves. [L81]
Pick the narrowest visibility that covers the runtime need, and sealed suits most dependencies. [L84]
The visibility vocabulary is inspired by CMake PUBLIC, PRIVATE and INTERFACE link visibility, as a memory aid only. [L88]
The order of the dependencies array is the canonical env composition order, and the first entry applies first. [L94]
Path entries from later dependencies are prepended onto earlier ones, while constant entries follow last-wins. [L94]
Put dependencies that should win near the end of the array, since the importing package env always emits last. [L96]
